formula.text: Scale factor = desired servings ÷ original servings. Scaled amount = original amount × scale factor. Tripling means a factor of 3.

howToSteps.name: Find the factor
howToSteps.text: Divide the servings you want by the servings the recipe makes. A recipe for 4 made for 12 has a factor of 3.

howToSteps.name: Multiply everything by 3
howToSteps.text: Work down the ingredient list and triple each amount. Flour, sugar, butter, liquids, and eggs all triple in full.

howToSteps.name: Hold back the leavening
howToSteps.text: Baking powder, baking soda, and yeast get about 2 1/4 times, not 3 times. Too much leavening makes bakes rise fast and sink.

howToSteps.name: Season in stages
howToSteps.text: Start salt and strong spices at about 2 1/4 times, then taste and add more. Big batches are easy to overseason.

howToSteps.name: Check the pot and pan
howToSteps.text: A tripled batch needs a much bigger vessel, or two of them. If the pot is too full, the food steams instead of browning.

title: How to Triple a Recipe: Scale by 3
tutorial: Tripling is the scaling I reach for when the freezer is the plan. A recipe for 4 becomes a recipe for 12: one dinner tonight, two in the freezer. The factor is 3, and the bulk ingredients triple in full. Two cups of flour become 6. One cup of beans becomes 3. Two eggs become 6. The maths is easy. The judgement is in the leavening, the seasoning, and the size of the pot.

Leavening is the first thing to hold back. The common rule of thumb when scaling up is to use about three-quarters of the linear amount of baking powder or soda, which means about 2 1/4 times when tripling, not 3 times. Too much leavening makes a cake rise fast and collapse in the middle, and it can leave a metallic taste that no amount of frosting hides. Salt and strong spices follow the same pattern: start at about 2 1/4 times, then taste and add more.

The second thing to check is the vessel. A tripled soup needs a pot three times the size, and most home kitchens do not have one. A pot that is too full steams instead of browning, and a tripled cake in the original pan will be three times as deep and may never set in the middle. Two batches are often the better answer: they cook more evenly, they are easier to handle, and one can go straight into the freezer.

Weighing helps at this size. Six cups of flour is faster and more accurate on a scale than in a measuring cup, and 9 eggs are easier to weigh than to count twice. A large egg is about 50 g out of the shell, so 9 eggs is about 450 g. If the recipe only gives cups, convert first, then scale. The numbers stay clean and the results stay consistent.

A tripled batch means leftovers by design, so plan the storage before you start cooking. Cool the extra portions quickly, pack them in the sizes you will actually reheat, and label each container with what it is and the date it went in. A freezer full of mystery containers is not meal prep. It is a science experiment.
